normalization.overview: Cole Medin argues that recurring coding-agent failures often call for small corrections in instructions, verification, context, authority, and scope rather than a new model or framework.
normalization.whyItMatters: His eleven examples are useful diagnostics, but their claimed payoff is not established by controlled comparisons. Real proof, effective permissions, and proportional validation still have to be tested.
normalization.ghostMeshTakeaway: Fix observed failures with the smallest enforceable existing control, preserve important human decisions, and measure the next normal task instead of adding eleven new mechanisms.
normalization.falsification: Compare matched ordinary agent tasks before and after one targeted harness change, including quality, review effort, elapsed time, changed scope and regression outcomes. The proposed trial has not been run.
normalization.freshness: November 10 creator video and private machine-ASR topic cues; platform documentation supports selected mechanisms, not performance payoffs.

claims.proposition: Real application journeys reveal defects missed by unit tests.

claims.proposition: Executable hooks can enforce selected prohibitions more reliably than prose-only rules.
claims.assessment: Specific intercepted tool events can be rejected; downstream authorization remains separate.
claims.limits: Hooks do not automatically cover alternate tools, subprocesses or credentials.

claims.proposition: Removing redundant global rules can improve agent focus.
claims.assessment: OpenAI recommends revisiting excessive instructions; no source-specific pruning benchmark is supplied.
claims.limits: Rare critical instructions must be preserved.

claims.proposition: Shorter task sessions and handoffs can reduce long-context deterioration.
claims.assessment: Plausible context-management practice, unquantified in this source.
claims.limits: Summaries can lose nuance and must not supplant retained evidence.

claims.proposition: Consequential product decisions should remain under human authority.
claims.assessment: A governance recommendation about decision scope, not an empirical performance result.
claims.limits: Routine bounded implementation should not require repetitive approval.

claims.proposition: Explicit boundaries can limit unwanted refactors on small tasks.
claims.assessment: Useful scope discipline; no controlled source benchmark.
claims.limits: Necessary dependency changes may still be justified.

claims.proposition: Deliberate subagent budgeting can reduce unnecessary usage.
claims.assessment: The creator offers cost-management advice without measured savings.
claims.limits: Independent parallel work can also reduce elapsed time.

claims.proposition: Test effort should reflect blast radius and consequence.
claims.assessment: Risk-proportional validation is a design principle, not a quantified study.
claims.limits: Small diffs may affect high-impact security boundaries.

claims.proposition: Parking unrelated discoveries helps agents finish the original task.
claims.assessment: Plausible focus discipline, with no controlled productivity evidence.
claims.limits: True blockers and urgent safety defects remain in scope.

archiveCall.label: Fix the failure before adding another layer
archiveCall.text: Keep this source as a practical checklist for diagnosing recurring coding-agent friction. Start with the observed failure, use the smallest existing control that can address it, and measure the next ordinary task. Do not install all eleven mechanisms by default.
